skill_title: Relate intermolecular forces to physical properties
notes: 20 items: 2 lifted-style, 18 fresh. Predict and explain trends in BP, MP, vapour pressure, surface tension, and solubility based on IMF strength.

items.question: How does INCREASING the strength of IMFs affect the BOILING POINT of a liquid?
items.expectedAnswer: Stronger IMFs ⇒ higher boiling point (more energy to separate molecules).
items.explanation: Stronger IMF = more energy to separate molecules = higher BP.
options: Stronger IMFs ⇒ higher boiling point (more energy to separate molecules).
Stronger IMFs ⇒ lower boiling point.
IMF strength has no effect on boiling point.

items.question: How does INCREASING the strength of IMFs affect the VAPOUR PRESSURE of a liquid?
items.expectedAnswer: Stronger IMFs ⇒ lower vapour pressure (fewer molecules escape).
items.explanation: Vapour pressure measures escaping tendency. Stronger IMF = less escape = lower VP.
options: Stronger IMFs ⇒ higher vapour pressure.
Stronger IMFs ⇒ lower vapour pressure (fewer molecules escape).
IMF strength has no effect on vapour pressure.

items.question: Compare the boiling points of CH₄, NH₃, and H₂O. Which has the highest BP and why?
items.expectedAnswer: H₂O — its extensive hydrogen bonding gives it the highest boiling point.
items.explanation: H₂O > NH₃ > CH₄. BP: 100°C > −33°C > −162°C. H₂O's tetrahedral H-bonding network is exceptional.
options: CH₄ — it is the smallest and lightest.
All three boil at the same temperature.
H₂O — its extensive hydrogen bonding gives it the highest boiling point.

items.question: Why is the BOILING POINT of butane HIGHER than that of methane?
items.expectedAnswer: Butane is larger (more electrons, more surface contact), so it has stronger London forces.
items.explanation: Larger molecule ⇒ stronger London. Within alkane series, BP rises with chain length.
options: Butane is larger (more electrons, more surface contact), so it has stronger London forces.
Because butane is polar and methane is not.
Because butane has hydrogen bonding.

items.question: How does INCREASING the strength of IMFs affect the SURFACE TENSION of a liquid?
items.expectedAnswer: Stronger IMFs ⇒ higher surface tension.
items.explanation: Surface tension ∝ IMF strength. Water 'beads up' more than oil because H-bonding > London.
options: Stronger IMFs ⇒ lower surface tension.
Stronger IMFs ⇒ higher surface tension.
IMF strength has no effect on surface tension.

items.question: How does a SOLUTE'S IMF compatibility with the SOLVENT affect SOLUBILITY?
items.expectedAnswer: 'Like dissolves like' — a solute dissolves best in a solvent with similar IMFs.
items.explanation: Solubility rule: like dissolves like. Same IMF type means good mixing.
options: Opposite IMF types dissolve best in each other.
IMF compatibility has no effect on solubility.
'Like dissolves like' — a solute dissolves best in a solvent with similar IMFs.

items.question: Why is the boiling point of ETHANOL much higher than that of DIETHYL ETHER, even though they have similar molecular masses?
items.expectedAnswer: Ethanol has hydrogen bonding (-OH); diethyl ether has no -OH, so only London + dipole-dipole.
items.explanation: H-bonding vs no H-bonding at similar size: H-bonding wins. Standard alcohol vs ether comparison.
options: Ethanol has hydrogen bonding (-OH); diethyl ether has no -OH, so only London + dipole-dipole.
Because diethyl ether is much larger than ethanol.
Because diethyl ether hydrogen bonds and ethanol doesn't.

items.question: Why does ICE have a LOWER DENSITY than liquid water?
items.expectedAnswer: Ice has an open hexagonal hydrogen-bonded lattice that spaces molecules farther apart.
items.explanation: Hydrogen-bonded crystal structure of ice has open hexagonal arrangement ⇒ less dense than liquid water.
options: Because ice molecules move faster than liquid water.
Ice has an open hexagonal hydrogen-bonded lattice that spaces molecules farther apart.
Because ice contains trapped air bubbles.

items.question: Rank the following in order of INCREASING boiling point: methane, ammonia, water.
items.expectedAnswer: Methane < ammonia < water.
items.explanation: IMF strength: London (CH₄) < H-bonding (NH₃) < extensive H-bonding (H₂O).
options: Water < ammonia < methane.
Methane < water < ammonia.
Methane < ammonia < water.

items.question: A learner says: 'Stronger IMFs always lead to higher vapour pressure.' Is this correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect — stronger IMFs hold molecules in the liquid, giving LOWER vapour pressure.
items.explanation: Common misconception. Vapour pressure ∝ ease of escape (inverse of IMF strength).
options: Incorrect — stronger IMFs hold molecules in the liquid, giving LOWER vapour pressure.
Correct — stronger forces push more molecules into the vapour.
Correct — vapour pressure and IMF strength are unrelated.

items.question: Why is sugar (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁) HIGHLY soluble in water but NOT in hexane (C₆H₁₄)?
items.expectedAnswer: Sugar has many -OH groups and hydrogen bonds with water ('like dissolves like'); hexane is non-polar.
items.explanation: Sugar has many H-bonding sites ⇒ readily H-bonds with water. Hexane: no H-bonding, no polarity, can't accommodate sugar.
options: Because sugar is non-polar like hexane.
Sugar has many -OH groups and hydrogen bonds with water ('like dissolves like'); hexane is non-polar.
Because hexane has stronger hydrogen bonding than water.

items.question: Why is oil insoluble in water?
items.expectedAnswer: Oil is non-polar (London only) while water is polar/H-bonded — unlike forces don't mix.
items.explanation: 'Like dissolves like.' Non-polar + polar = incompatible.
options: Because oil is denser than water.
Because oil hydrogen bonds too strongly with itself.
Oil is non-polar (London only) while water is polar/H-bonded — unlike forces don't mix.

items.question: Compare boiling points of CH₃F (methyl fluoride) and CH₃CH₃ (ethane). Which is higher and why?
items.expectedAnswer: CH₃F — it is polar (dipole-dipole), whereas ethane has only London forces.
items.explanation: Polar molecule beats non-polar of similar size. CH₃F adds dipole-dipole on top of London.
options: CH₃F — it is polar (dipole-dipole), whereas ethane has only London forces.
Ethane — it has hydrogen bonding.
Equal — both have only London forces.

items.question: Which substance is expected to have the highest melting point: I₂, F₂, Br₂, Cl₂?
options: I₂
Br₂
Cl₂
F₂
items.expectedAnswer: I₂
items.explanation: All are non-polar diatomic halogens (London only). I₂ is the largest (most electrons) ⇒ strongest London ⇒ highest MP. (F₂: −220°C, Cl₂: −101°C, Br₂: −7°C, I₂: 114°C — solid at room T.)

items.question: Why does water have an UNUSUALLY HIGH boiling point compared to other small hydrides like H₂S, H₂Se, H₂Te (which have lower BPs despite being heavier)?
items.expectedAnswer: H₂O can hydrogen bond (H on O), which is far stronger than the forces in H₂S, H₂Se, H₂Te.
items.explanation: H-bonding overrides the size trend. Famous BP anomaly: H₂O sticks above the line.
options: Because water is the heaviest of the group.
H₂O can hydrogen bond (H on O), which is far stronger than the forces in H₂S, H₂Se, H₂Te.
Because water is non-polar.

items.question: Two compounds have the same molecular formula but different shapes: one is more compact (branched), the other is more elongated (straight chain). Which has the higher boiling point?
items.expectedAnswer: The elongated (straight-chain) molecule — more surface contact gives stronger London forces.
items.explanation: Surface area ↑ ⇒ London ↑ ⇒ BP ↑. Straight chains > branched.
options: The compact (branched) one — it packs more tightly.
Equal — the same formula means the same boiling point.
The elongated (straight-chain) molecule — more surface contact gives stronger London forces.

items.question: Why are LONDON forces alone sufficient to make large non-polar molecules SOLIDS at room temperature (like wax, polythene)?
items.expectedAnswer: With many electrons and large surface area, the cumulative London forces become large.
items.explanation: Many small forces add up. Long alkane chains = strong total London = solids.
options: With many electrons and large surface area, the cumulative London forces become large.
Because large non-polar molecules develop hydrogen bonding.
Because London forces are individually very strong.

items.question: Why does isopropanol ((CH₃)₂CHOH) evaporate more quickly than water at room temperature?
items.expectedAnswer: Isopropanol has only one -OH and is bulkier, so less extensive H-bonding ⇒ higher vapour pressure.
items.explanation: Per-molecule H-bonding: water > isopropanol (water can be both donor and acceptor more times).
options: Because isopropanol has no hydrogen bonding at all.
Isopropanol has only one -OH and is bulkier, so less extensive H-bonding ⇒ higher vapour pressure.
Because isopropanol has stronger IMFs than water.

items.question: Predict and explain the order of MELTING POINT: NaCl (ionic), H₂O (H-bonding), CH₄ (London only).
items.expectedAnswer: NaCl > H₂O > CH₄ (ionic bonding > hydrogen bonding > London only).
items.explanation: Ionic >> H-bonding > London. Reflects bond energies: ~hundreds of kJ/mol (ionic) vs ~tens (H-bonding) vs ~few (London).
options: CH₄ > H₂O > NaCl.
H₂O > NaCl > CH₄.
NaCl > H₂O > CH₄ (ionic bonding > hydrogen bonding > London only).

items.question: Two compounds A and B have molecular masses 58 g/mol and 60 g/mol respectively. A boils at −0.5°C; B boils at 97°C. Suggest what IMFs are at work in each.
items.expectedAnswer: A has only London (e.g. butane); B has hydrogen bonding (e.g. propan-1-ol), giving its much higher BP.
items.explanation: Diagnostic: similar MM but big BP difference ⇒ one has H-bonding. Classic alkane vs alcohol comparison.
options: A has only London (e.g. butane); B has hydrogen bonding (e.g. propan-1-ol), giving its much higher BP.
A has hydrogen bonding; B has only London forces.
Both have identical IMFs since their masses are similar.
